## Audience

Public-health analysts and partners briefing on BMI differences across income groups in a classroom NHANES equity dataset.

## Slide 1: Context

**Question:** How does mean BMI differ by income group among adults age 20-80 in the prepared classroom NHANES equity dataset, and why does the pattern matter for a public-health discussion?

The result matters because analysts need a concise, descriptive comparison before deciding whether further, survey-weighted analysis or a policy conversation is warranted.

## Slide 2: Evidence

Table 1 from Assignment 6 summarizes complete records in the age 20-80 cohort:

| Income group | N | Mean BMI (SD) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Low Income (<1.3) | 15,293 | 29.4 (7.5) |
| Middle Income | 19,228 | 29.3 (7.0) |
| High Income (>3.5) | 16,330 | 28.6 (6.3) |

The low- and middle-income groups have nearly the same mean BMI, while the high-income group has a mean 0.7-0.8 kg/m2 lower.

Source: `../assignment06-eda-ai-audit/submission/table1.csv` and [CDC/NCHS NHANES public-use data](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/) used for the classroom example.

## Slide 3: Takeaway

In this classroom dataset, BMI means are similar in the low- and middle-income groups and lowest in the high-income group.

## Slide 4: Limitation

This is a descriptive, unweighted complete-case summary of a prepared classroom dataset. It cannot establish population-level differences or show that income causes BMI differences.

## Slide 5: Next Step

An analyst could discuss whether a survey-weighted, covariate-adjusted analysis would help, and a public-health partner could identify factors or interventions that should be investigated rather than inferred from this summary.
